strengths: The paper is framed appropriately as an Applied/Systems contribution: it presents a modular, high-performance implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting training, and it is judged here on engineering merit rather than algorithmic novelty.

The motivation section is grounded in careful profiling (warp cycles per instruction, L2 cache hit rate, MIO/LG throttle analysis) that clearly identifies concrete GPU bottlenecks (atomic contention, poor spatial locality, coarse bounding boxes) rather than relying on generic claims.

The proposed techniques (cluster/compact via Morton code, tighter 2D AABBs with variable tile size, shared-memory multi-batch reduction, sparse gradients) are sensible engineering responses to the diagnosed bottlenecks, and each is individually illustrated with supporting measurements (Figs. 5-7).

Reported results show a substantial 3.4x speedup over vanilla 3DGS and 1.4x over the TamingGS-accelerated baseline, with comparable or slightly better PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on Mip-NeRF 360, suggesting the optimizations do not sacrifice quality.

The critical discussion of the sparse Adam claim in Taming-GS (attributing the speedup to fused rather than sparse computation) reflects a careful, evidence-based engineering analysis rather than uncritical adoption of prior tricks.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly identifies gsplat [22] as the closest prior work in usability/modularity, and Figure 1 visually claims LiteGS dominates it, yet no quantitative comparison (speed, memory, or quality) against gsplat is provided anywhere in the evaluation, leaving the central competitive claim unsubstantiated.

Evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360); no results on Tanks & Temples or Deep Blending (used in the original 3DGS paper) or other benchmarks are given, limiting confidence in generality of the speedup and quality claims.

The authors note they 'applied specific processing and parameter adjustments to the SfM step' for COLMAP results, which alters the baseline 3DGS numbers relative to the original paper; this raises concerns about whether the speed/quality comparison between 3DGS and LiteGS is conducted on strictly identical preprocessing, affecting reproducibility and fairness of comparison.

No breakdown/ablation table quantifies the individual contribution of each proposed technique (clustering, tighter AABB, 8x8 tiling, reduction algorithm) to the overall 3.4x speedup; the qualitative figures (patch counts, fragment counts, L2 hit rate) are suggestive but do not translate into an end-to-end wall-clock ablation.
The code repository link is blank in the submitted manuscript, undermining the reproducibility that is central to a systems/tools contribution.
Memory reduction (~30%) is stated in the abstract but never substantiated with a table or figure in the body of the paper.

The technical novelty is primarily the integration of known techniques (Morton-code spatial sorting, cluster culling/compaction, tighter bounding boxes, shared-memory reduction, sparse gradients from prior work) rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas; this is acceptable for a systems paper but should be more explicitly acknowledged, and the incremental nature limits broader scientific contribution beyond the specific 3DGS use case.
Minor writing issues (typos such as 'simpling', 'Synchroniz', inconsistent grammar, unclear figure captions) reduce clarity and polish expected for publication.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important practical problem: the original 3DGS CUDA implementation is slow and hard to modify, and the paper provides a thorough, well-motivated profiling analysis (warp cycles per instruction, MIO/LG throttle analysis, L2 cache hit rate degradation) that clearly diagnoses real bottlenecks in backward rasterization and memory locality.

The proposed engineering solutions (cluster-based culling/compaction via Morton codes, tighter 2D AABBs considering both axes and opacity, smaller 8x8 tiles, multi-batch shared-memory reduction to replace AtomicAdd) are sensible, individually well-justified by the preceding profiling evidence, and together produce a reported 3.4x end-to-end speedup with ~30% memory reduction while maintaining rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS comparable or slightly better than vanilla 3DGS).

The dual API design (Python/autograd for prototyping, CUDA extension for production) targets a real usability gap in the 3DGS ecosystem and could have practical value for the community if released as working open-source software.

The critique of TamingGS's sparse-Adam claim (arguing the speedup is mainly from the fused-kernel component rather than sparsity per se) is an interesting and potentially useful empirical observation for practitioners.
weaknesses: No ablation study isolating the contribution of each individual technique (clustering/compaction, tighter AABB, 8x8 tiling, reduction algorithm) to the overall 3.4x speedup; only aggregate end-to-end numbers are given, making it impossible to assess which optimizations matter most or whether they are complementary or redundant.

The most directly relevant and heavily-cited competitor, gsplat (cited as the only other modular/usable 3DGS library and prominently plotted in Figure 1), is never included in the actual quantitative speed or quality comparison tables (Table 2/3); likewise DISTWAR and OctreeGS appear in Figure 1 but not in any benchmark. This omission significantly weakens the core efficiency claims, since the paper only compares against vanilla 3DGS and a TamingGS-integrated variant.

Reported 3DGS quality numbers were obtained after the authors applied unspecified 'specific processing and parameter adjustments' to the COLMAP/SfM step, which is explicitly stated to raise 3DGS's metrics above those in the original paper; this ad-hoc, underspecified preprocessing change undermines reproducibility and fair comparison, and it is unclear whether LiteGS benefits from the same adjustments equally.
No code/repository link is actually provided (the 'available at' sentence is left blank), undermining reproducibility despite claims of an open, modular framework.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360); no results on Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, or other standard 3DGS benchmarks that would test generalization of the speedups and quality preservation.
The claimed 30% memory reduction from the abstract is never substantiated with actual measured numbers/tables in the body of the paper.

The manuscript has notable writing/presentation issues inappropriate for a final submission: inconsistent/lowercase section headers ('clustering', 'cluster culling&compacting', 'more accurate 2D AABB'), an empty Figure 1 caption, run-on and occasionally ungrammatical sentences, and informal phrasing ('we use more tricks') that reduce clarity and polish.

Technical novelty is limited: most individual components (Morton-code spatial sorting, AABB tightening, cluster-based culling, shared-memory reduction to avoid atomics) are well-known GPU optimization techniques adapted to the 3DGS pipeline rather than new algorithmic contributions; this is acceptable for a systems paper but the paper does not clearly position its contribution relative to this being primarily an engineering effort, nor discuss limitations (e.g., scalability to larger/more complex scenes, dynamic scenes, or non-NVIDIA hardware).

strengths: The paper provides a thorough, data-driven systems analysis of 3DGS training bottlenecks (warp-cycle profiling, MIO/LG throttle analysis, L2 cache hit-rate degradation), which convincingly motivates each subsequent design decision rather than presenting optimizations ad hoc.

The reported speedups are substantial and practically meaningful: 3.4x over vanilla 3DGS and 1.4x over the strong TamingGS-accelerated baseline, with quality metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) on Mip-NeRF 360 maintained or slightly improved, suggesting the engineering gains are not achieved at the cost of accuracy.

The dual-API design (Python/autograd for prototyping, CUDA extensions for production) addresses a genuine usability gap in the 3DGS ecosystem and, if released, could be a useful community tool for research productivity.

Individual optimizations are each supported with targeted micro-benchmarks (e.g., patch-count reduction from tighter AABBs in Fig. 6, fragment-count reduction from 8x8 tiling in Fig. 7, L2 hit-rate preservation from cluster+compact in Fig. 5), giving readers insight into where the gains come from.

The discussion correcting the misattribution of TamingGS's sparse-Adam speedup (showing it is largely due to the fused-kernel implementation rather than sparsity per se) is a valuable, honest clarification for the community.
weaknesses: No end-to-end ablation table quantifying the individual contribution of each proposed component (clustering, cluster culling/compacting, tighter AABB, 8x8 tiling, reduction algorithm) to the overall 3.4x speedup; only indirect proxy metrics (cache hit rate, patch/fragment counts) are shown per-component, making it hard to assess where most of the benefit comes from.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360); no results on Tanks & Temples or Deep Blending (used in the original 3DGS paper) or other common benchmarks, limiting confidence in generalization.

No quantitative comparison against gsplat or other modular/efficient 3DGS libraries mentioned in Related Work and depicted qualitatively in Figure 1; the comparison is only against vanilla 3DGS and the TamingGS-integrated variant.
The code repository link in Section 4 is left blank/unfilled ("The full source code is available at ."), which undermines reproducibility claims at submission time.

The paper focuses exclusively on training-time speedup; no analysis of rendering/inference throughput, memory usage breakdown beyond the aggregate 30% figure, or robustness of speed results across multiple runs (variance/standard deviation not reported).

Baseline 3DGS numbers are obtained with modified COLMAP/SfM preprocessing that differs from the original paper, which is only briefly justified; this could raise concerns about a fair apples-to-apples comparison even though it nominally affects both methods equally.

Writing quality and structure could be improved (inconsistent section-heading capitalization, some grammatical issues), and the usability/prototyping benefit of the modular API is asserted but not empirically demonstrated (e.g., via a case study of adding a new feature or a user study).

strengths: Comprehensive system+algorithm co-design spanning low-level GPU kernel optimization (warp-based raster with scanline reformulation and mixed precision), mid-level data management (Morton-code based cluster-cull-compact), and high-level algorithm design (opacity gradient variance densification metric and opacity decay), providing a holistic pipeline rather than a single-point optimization.

Strong empirical results across three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) showing substantial speedups (up to 13.4x vs 3DGS, 1.4x vs Mini-Splatting v2) while achieving comparable or better quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), and Pareto-dominant trade-offs at multiple parameter/quality scales (turbo/balance/quality variants).

Detailed, well-isolated ablation studies (Tables 2-4) that separately quantify the contribution of Cluster-Cull-Compact, the warp-based rasterizer (with fine-grained forward/backward timing breakdowns against atomic, per-splat, and tensor-core rasterizers), and the densification strategy (decay vs. variance metric), lending credibility to the individual claimed contributions.

Technical explanations of the warp-based rasterizer and scanline algorithm are detailed with clear derivations (reducing register/variable usage from 7 to 3, multiplications from 9 to 3), giving good insight into why speedups occur, which aids reproducibility for those familiar with GPU kernel design.
The work is positioned as an open-source framework, which if released as claimed, would provide practical value to the community for fast 3DGS training on commodity GPUs.

The paper is generally well organized, following a layered structure (system layer, data layer, algorithm layer) that mirrors its narrative of a full pipeline redesign, making the contributions easy to follow section by section.
weaknesses: The opacity gradient variance metric intuition (high variance indicates a genuine under-reconstructed region) is plausible but not rigorously justified theoretically or via targeted qualitative visualizations (e.g., heatmaps comparing variance-based vs. gradient-magnitude-based selection on actual scenes); the ablation only reports aggregate PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS differences without deeper analysis of why/where the metric helps.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different training iteration counts (e.g., SSS at 40K vs. LiteGS variants at 30K, marked with asterisks) which complicates fair comparison; while the text partially addresses this by also reporting LiteGS-quality at 30K iterations, the presentation remains somewhat inconsistent and could confuse readers trying to compare wall-clock efficiency fairly.

All experiments are conducted on a single GPU type (RTX 3090); no evidence is given for portability/generalization of the warp-based rasterizer and mixed-precision optimizations to other GPU architectures (e.g., non-NVIDIA hardware, older/newer NVIDIA generations, mobile GPUs), despite claims about applicability to 'major commercial GPUs.'

The novelty of individual components is somewhat incremental relative to prior art: warp-based reduction is an evolution of DISTWAR/Taming3DGS/TC-GS optimizations, cluster-cull-compact is a direct adaptation of established real-time rendering techniques (BVH/Nanite-style clustering) using Morton codes, which is a well known and simple technique; the main contribution is the integration and engineering rather than fundamentally new algorithmic insight.

No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or repeated-run statistics are reported for the quantitative comparisons, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS gains, especially the smaller gains (0.2-0.4 dB) claimed as a 'new accuracy record.'

The paper does not clearly discuss failure cases, scenes where the method underperforms, or the sensitivity of hyperparameters (e.g., cluster size of 128, decay every 10 epochs, densification interval of 5 epochs) to different scene types or datasets, limiting insight into robustness and generality of the chosen design points.

While the paper states the framework is open-sourced, no link, anonymized repository, or code availability details are provided in the submission for verification during review, raising reproducibility concerns given the low-level, hardware-specific nature of the kernel optimizations described.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important problem—3DGS training cost—with a holistic systems+algorithm co-design spanning GPU kernel design, data layout, and densification criteria, rather than a single-point optimization.

The warp-based rasterizer with scanline reformulation and mixed-precision reduction is a concrete, well-motivated kernel-level contribution, and Table 3 shows substantial speedups over atomic, per-splat, and tensor-core rasterizers across multiple primitive scales.

The Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline is a sensible adaptation of established real-time-rendering locality techniques to the dynamic 3DGS training setting, and is shown to be orthogonal to sparse-gradient update strategies.

The opacity-gradient-variance densification criterion is intuitively motivated (distinguishing genuine under-reconstruction from unconverged-but-adequate regions) and its computation is cheaply piggybacked on the proposed rasterizer's statistics gathering.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical results across three standard datasets (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) and three operating points (turbo/balance/quality) show competitive or superior PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS at markedly reduced training time versus 3DGS, 3DGS-MCMC, TamingGS, Mini-Splatting(v2), and SSS.

Ablations isolate the contribution of Cluster-Cull-Compact, the warp-based rasterizer, and each densification component (opacity decay, variance metric), providing some evidence of the necessity of each module.
The framework is stated to be open-sourced, which aids reproducibility if released as promised.
weaknesses: The claimed 'subminute'/'minute-level' training headline is not well substantiated by the main results table: the fastest reported configuration (LiteGS-turbo) still takes 108-145 seconds, and the 'quality' configuration takes 330-515 seconds (5-9 minutes); the subminute framing in the title and abstract appears to oversell results relative to what is empirically shown, with only a speculative aside about 'possibly second-level on RTX 5090' that is not tested.

Statistical rigor is weak: no error bars, variance across runs, or multiple seeds are reported for any table, despite 3DGS training being known to have run-to-run variability; single-run numbers reported to two decimal places risk conveying false precision, particularly for close comparisons (e.g., 0.2-0.4 dB PSNR gains).

Hardware generality is unclear—mixed-precision and integer warp-reduce tricks are tuned for a single RTX 3090 and described as relying on 'NVIDIA Ampere and newer' features; no cross-GPU validation (e.g., different register files, warp sizes, or AMD/other vendors) is provided, limiting confidence in the generality of the 'optimal tile size/pixels-per-thread' tuning claims.

The opacity-gradient variance metric and opacity-decay mechanism, while intuitively justified, lack any theoretical or statistical grounding (e.g., no analysis of estimator bias/consistency, no sensitivity study over decay schedule or variance threshold choices beyond the fixed hyperparameters used); the ablation in Table 4 only shows end-result deltas without deeper diagnostic analysis of why variance outperforms the per-pixel-error baseline.

Comparisons are somewhat inconsistent in iteration counts/budgets across rows (e.g., SSS at 40K iterations vs. others at 30K, with an asterisked caveat), which complicates a fully fair comparison and could partly explain some of the quality gaps; the rationale for matching SSS's 40K iteration setting while reporting a separate 30K number only for LiteGS-quality is not clearly justified.

The novelty of individual components is somewhat incremental when viewed separately: warp-based single-reduction rasterization, Morton-order spatial sorting for locality, and gradient-variance-based densification criteria are each natural extensions of well-known techniques (warp-level reduction, Z-order curves in real-time rendering, uncertainty-aware splitting criteria in prior 3DGS works); the main contribution is integration/engineering rather than fundamentally new algorithmic insight, which should be acknowledged more explicitly.

Clarity issues: notation is dense and occasionally inconsistent (e.g., mixing of index notation for Morton code bit interleaving, unclear precise definition of 'quasi-stable state'), and some claims (e.g., the specific thread/tile configuration being 'optimal') are asserted without an ablation sweep showing the design space explored.

No analysis of failure cases or limitations of the new densification/rasterization approach on more challenging scenes (e.g., highly reflective, thin structures, or unbounded scenes with extreme depth complexity) is provided, despite the paper's claims of being a 'new performance benchmark for the field.'

Memory footprint and peak memory claims are only qualitatively asserted (e.g., 'lower peak memory footprint' versus Mini-Splatting) without quantitative measurements, which weakens a stated practical advantage.

strengths: The paper tackles the well-recognized training efficiency bottleneck of 3DGS with a genuinely holistic system+algorithm codesign spanning three levels (low-level GPU kernel, mid-level data layout, high-level densification algorithm), which is a more complete treatment than most prior single-aspect acceleration works.

The warp-based rasterizer is a well-motivated and clearly explained technical contribution: reducing per-tile gradient reduction to a single warp reduction, combined with a scanline reformulation of the Gaussian exponent to cut register usage, and a hardware-aware mixed-precision/integer warp-reduce trick for covariance gradients. The microbenchmark in Table 3 convincingly isolates and quantifies this contribution against atomic, per-splat, and tensor-core baselines, showing consistent and substantial speedups.

The Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline is a lightweight and practical adaptation of a real-time-rendering idea (Morton-code sorting + cluster-level culling/compaction) to the 3DGS training loop, and its benefit is cleanly isolated in an ablation (Table 2) showing large training-time reduction with negligible quality loss.

The opacity-gradient-variance densification metric is a reasonable statistical rationale (distinguishing unconverged-but-consistent gradients from genuinely conflicting/under-reconstructed regions) and is shown to be cheaply computable as a byproduct of the rasterizer's per-pixel statistics gathering; the paired opacity-decay mechanism is a sensible refinement over hard resets, and both components are individually ablated (Table 4).

End-to-end results are strong and span multiple operating points (turbo/balance/quality), demonstrating Pareto-optimal trade-offs against a broad and current set of baselines (3DGS, TamingGS, Mini-Splatting/v2, 3DGS-MCMC, SSS) across three standard datasets, with up to 13.4x speedup over vanilla 3DGS and competitive-to-superior PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS at greatly reduced parameter counts and training time.
The framework is reported to be open-sourced, aiding reproducibility and community adoption, which is valuable for an engineering/systems-oriented contribution of this kind.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single GPU (RTX 3090); claims about the generalizability of hardware-specific tricks (e.g., the integer warp-reduce accumulation trick, optimal tile size of 128, 4 pixels/thread) to 'major commercial GPUs' are asserted but not empirically validated across different architectures or vendors (e.g., newer NVIDIA generations, AMD GPUs).

Results appear to be single-run numbers with no reported variance, standard deviation, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (sometimes modest, e.g., 0.2-0.4 dB PSNR) improvements over strong baselines like 3DGS-MCMC and SSS.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different iteration budgets (18K/30K/40K, denoted by asterisks) across methods; while the authors partially address this by matching iterations to SSS for one setting, the overall table remains somewhat heterogeneous and could benefit from a cleaner iso-iteration or iso-time comparison for all rows.

LPIPS is occasionally worse than competing methods (e.g., LiteGS-turbo vs. Mini-Splatting/v2) despite PSNR gains, and this trade-off (attributed to fewer points capturing less high-frequency detail) is only briefly acknowledged rather than analyzed in depth (e.g., via qualitative visual comparisons or texture-detail analysis).

The paper claims a lower peak memory footprint as an advantage over aggressive densify-and-prune baselines like Mini-Splatting, but no quantitative peak-memory measurements are provided to substantiate this claim.

The three ablation studies (rasterizer, cluster-cull-compact, densification) are conducted mostly in isolation; a combined/joint ablation showing how the three levels of optimization interact (e.g., whether cluster-level locality also benefits the densification metric computation, or whether disabling one component changes the benefit of another) is not provided.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'Relate Work' section title typo, 'signle' typo, some inconsistent notation) suggest the manuscript would benefit from an additional proofreading pass.
